title: Egungun and the Voice of Oro
subtitle: Ancestors and community in a colonial-era report

learningObjectives.text: What does Ellis say the word Egungun means?

egungun.work: The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa
egungun.author: A. B. Ellis
egungun.translator: not applicable; authored in English by A. B. Ellis
egungun.locator: Chapter VI · EGUNGUN, ORO, ABIKU, AND VARIOUS SUPERSTITIONS; Chapter VI · EGUNGUN, ORO, ABIKU, AND VARIOUS SUPERSTITIONS, normalized characters 68-1085
egungun.excerpt: EGUNGUN really means "bone," hence "skeleton," and Egungun himself is supposed to be a man risen from the dead. The part is acted by a man disguised in a long robe, usually made of grass, and a mask of wood, which generally represents a hideous human face, with a long pointed nose and thin lips, but sometimes the head of an animal. Egungun appears in the streets by day or night indifferently, leaping, dancing, or walking grotesquely, and uttering loud cries. He is supposed to have returned from the land of the dead in order to ascertain what is going on in the land of the living, and his function is to carry away those persons who are troublesome to their neighbors. He may thus be considered a kind of supernatitral inquisitor who appears from time to time to inquire into the general domestic conduct of people, particularly of women, and to punish misdeeds. Although it is very well known that Egungun is only a disguised man, yet it is popularly believed that to touch him, even by accident, causes death.
egungun.note: Verbatim English text from Ellis's 1894 survey of the Yoruba-speaking peoples. It is colonial-era ethnography: claims belong to Ellis's report, and his comparative and evolutionary framing is commentary, not community testimony.

oro.excerpt: The word Oro means fierceness, tempest, or provocation, and Oro himself appears to be personified executive power. Oro is supposed to haunt the forest in the neighbourhood of towns, and he makes his approach known by a strange, whirring, roaring noise. As soon as this is heard, all women must shut themselves up in their houses, and refrain from looking out on pain of death. The voice of Oro is produced by whirling round and round a thin strip of wood, some 21/2 inches broad, 12 inches long, and tapering at both ends, which is fastened to a stick by a long string.
oro.note: Verbatim English text from Ellis's 1894 survey of the Yoruba-speaking peoples. It is colonial-era ethnography: claims belong to Ellis's report, and his comparative and evolutionary framing is commentary, not community testimony.

narrativeBlocks.title: A figure named for bone
narrativeBlocks.body: Ellis reports that Egungun means “bone,” hence “skeleton”: a performer in a long grass robe and wooden mask plays a man risen from the dead.

narrativeBlocks.title: The dead inspect the living

narrativeBlocks.title: Everyone knows, and still steps back
narrativeBlocks.body: Ellis notes it is “very well known” that Egungun is only a disguised man, yet people believe even an accidental touch causes death, and crowds scatter when he rushes toward them.

narrativeBlocks.title: An outside reporter's apparatus
narrativeBlocks.body: Ellis openly describes the costume, the performer, and the crowd's reaction. That is an 1894 observer explaining how the figure is made, not testimony from inside the institution.

narrativeBlocks.title: Oro's hidden voice
narrativeBlocks.body: In the same chapter Ellis describes Oro as “personified executive power.” Its voice is the whirring roar of a slat of wood spun on a string, a bull-roarer, and women were required to stay indoors when it sounded. Two figures, two different relationships between the community and the unseen.
